# How guarded writes prevent clobbering

When two people (or two agents) read the same role, policy, or tension and then
both write it back, the second write can silently erase the first — a *clobber*.
This document explains how the CLI guards against that: how it captures a
resource's version when you read it, sends that version back as a precondition
when you write, and surfaces the server's refusal in a way an operator or agent
can act on. The mechanism is optimistic concurrency built on HTTP `ETag` /
`If-Match`, and it is deliberately split into three independent pieces.

## Why capture, guard, and surface are three separate mechanisms

You might expect one "safe write" feature. Instead the CLI has three:

- **Version capture** — reading a single resource records its version (the
  `ETag`) in-process.
- **Guarded write** — a write can send that version back as an `If-Match`
  precondition, so the server rejects the write if the resource changed in the
  meantime.
- **Stale-write surfacing** — a rejected guarded write (`412 Precondition
  Failed`) is reported as its own failure category with its own exit code.

They were split on purpose. Each is a shared *mechanism* that lives in the
client foundation, not in any one command. Bundling them — or wiring them
straight into `tension update` — would couple a general capability to a specific
command and inflate each change with the others' behavior and tests. The
alternative considered for each piece was "retrofit the existing commands now";
it was rejected every time in favor of shipping the mechanism first and letting
each write command opt in later (the same capture-then-send-then-surface split
the roadmap draws, mirroring the earlier resolver → call-site-retrofit
precedent). The consequence is a clean boundary: version capture reads, the
guarded write sends, stale-write surfacing reports — and no piece has to reason
about another's surface.

## Why the version is captured verbatim and never interpreted

A resource's version lives only in the `ETag` response header — Glassfrog v5
resources carry no `version` field in the body. The CLI reads it through a small
accessor and returns it **exactly as the server sent it**: no unquoting, no
stripping of weak-validator (`W/"…"`) markers, no normalization of any kind.

The reason is subtle but decisive. An `ETag` is an opaque server fingerprint.
The only thing that makes a later `If-Match` succeed is echoing back *precisely*
the token the server issued. Any reshaping — even something as innocent-looking
as removing surrounding quotes — risks the server seeing a token it never issued
and refusing a write that should have succeeded (a spurious `412`). So the
verbatim guarantee is fixed at the point of capture, and the guarded write
forwards the value straight to the `If-Match` header with no transformation. A
maintainer who simply threads the captured version through to the write is
correct by default.

For the same reason the CLI never captures a version from **list** reads. A
collection's `ETag` fingerprints the whole collection, not any single item;
retaining it would invite guarding a single-resource write with a value that
cannot apply to it.

## Why an absent version means "write unconditionally," not "fail"

Many responses legitimately carry no `ETag`. The CLI treats an absent version and
an empty one identically: both mean "there is nothing to guard with." A read
that returns no version still succeeds — a read must never depend on a
concurrency token it does not need. And a write with no version sends **no**
`If-Match` header at all, so it proceeds unconditionally, exactly as writes did
before this machinery existed.

This "empty-as-absent" symmetry is what keeps the whole surface
behavior-preserving. Until a command deliberately opts in by supplying a
captured version, every existing read and write is byte-identical to what it was
before. The alternative — sending an empty or fabricated precondition when none
was captured — would invite spurious `412`s and break the unconditional
last-write-wins path the API documents for an omitted `If-Match`.

## Why a clobber gets its own exit code

When a guarded write is refused, the server returns `412 Precondition Failed`.
The CLI could have left that in the generic API-error bucket (exit code `3`),
distinguished only by its message text. It doesn't. A `412` is mapped to its own
failure category, **stale-write**, carrying a new exit code — `7`.

The driving scenario is an agent operator that branches on `$?`. If a clobber
shared exit code `3` with every other uncategorized non-2xx (a `404`, a `500`),
an agent could not tell "the resource changed under me, re-read and retry" from
"that thing doesn't exist" without parsing text — exactly what the exit-code
convention exists to avoid. A distinct code makes the clobber machine-detectable:
`$?` == `7` means clobber, and the agent can re-read and retry on its own.

Code `7` is the first value added beyond the originally-published `0`–`6` band,
but this is the convention's own extension rule at work — a new category takes
the next unused code, and no existing code is ever renumbered or reassigned, so
every consumer's existing branch on `$?` keeps its meaning. The same refusal also
gets a `412`-specific *cause* ("the resource changed since it was read") and a
*next step* ("re-read the resource for its current version, then retry"),
replacing the generic "check that the token has access" hint that is simply wrong
for a stale write — it was a write, not a read, and the token is fine.

## Why classification depends only on the status

The stale-write category is decided by **one thing**: the surfaced `412`. It does
not depend on whether this CLI actually sent an `If-Match`, on which command
failed, or on which resource was targeted. This mirrors exactly how `401`, `403`,
and `429` are classified — by status alone.

Keeping classification status-only is what lets the three mechanisms stay
decoupled. If the surfacing code had to know that a guarded write was in flight,
it would become per-command logic instead of one shared branch, and the clean
capture → guard → surface boundary would collapse. Classifying by status keeps
one mechanism serving every write, present and future.

## Design boundaries

These mechanisms deliberately stop short of several things a "smarter" tool
might do:

- **No automatic recovery.** A stale write is surfaced, not retried. The CLI does
  not re-read, retry, or back off on a `412` — doing so would hide the very
  clobber the code exists to make visible, and would re-introduce the
  unbounded-recovery hazard the failure pipeline keeps out of the classifier. The
  operator (or a future per-command read-then-retry flow) decides what to do.
- **No persistence.** A captured version is never written to disk or config. It is
  valid only against the resource state read in the current process; a persisted
  version would be stale by the next invocation and would defeat the guard it
  exists to enable.
- **No version in operator-facing output.** The captured version never appears in
  `json`, `yaml`, `full`, or `compact` output. It is internal plumbing consumed
  in-process by a guarded write, not a field for the operator; surfacing it would
  change a settled read contract for no benefit.
- **No change to any other status.** Stale-write surfacing is an additive branch
  off the generic bucket. No status other than `412` has its category, cause, next
  step, or exit code changed — altering another would be an unrequested behavior
  change across the whole failure surface.
- **No fabricated cause.** When the API supplies its own detail, that detail is
  surfaced; when it does not, the cause states only what the `412` status itself
  means (a precondition failed because the resource changed since it was read). It
  never invents a specific reason — or names *who* changed the resource — that the
  failure does not support.
